notes: Two call types alternate: one peaking around 32 kHz and one around 40 kHz, with different curvature. Both keys describe this alternation; sometimes only the lower call is recorded. The whole call band runs from about 45 kHz down to about 29 kHz (Bristol: 46.0 to 28.4 kHz; the Bedfordshire key hears the calls between 30 and 45 kHz). Per-call start and end values are not separately sourced, so the end of the high call is left out and its last shape point (35 kHz) is a drawing choice. The Bristol page gives a power-spectrum peak of 56 kHz, which disagrees with both keys and was not used. Duration and interval left out (single source). Calls are short and rapid, like impatient knocking.

notes: Steep sweep that flattens into a tail near 27 to 30 kHz. The Bedfordshire key gives a peak of 27 to 32 kHz and an irregular rhythm of about 10 calls a second; the Iberian key only groups it with Nyctalus and Vespertilio at 20 to 30 kHz, so the peak is agreed only up to about 30 kHz and the maximum is left out. End 28 kHz is from the Bristol minimum (27.7 kHz) and the key's statement that the loud tail holds the peak. Interval 110 ms: Bristol mean 116 ms, key about 100 ms. Duration left out (Bristol: 5.2 ms, no second source). The shape's first point (57 kHz) is one measured value. Noctule and Leisler's bat are lower; barbastelle and long-eared bats can mimic it.

notes: Short FM sweep with no flat tail; the call sounds like a click on a detector. Whiskered, Brandt's and Natterer's bats overlap and are hard to separate by call alone. Start 61 kHz is one measured value (Bristol) that the Bedfordshire key only supports loosely (calls audible up to at least 60 kHz); end 38 kHz is supported by the Bristol minimum and the Raleigh table's 35 to 39 kHz. The Raleigh table gives a peak of 35 to 39 kHz, which disagrees with the Bristol peak of about 50 kHz and the Iberian key's 45 to 70 kHz for FM-only Myotis, so that table's figure was not used for the peak. Duration 6 ms sits at the top of the Raleigh 2 to 6 ms range. Interval 70 ms is supported by the Bristol mean (69.8 ms), the key's 11 to 14 calls a second (71 to 91 ms) and the table's 28 to 75 ms.

notes: Noctules often alternate a higher and a lower call (a 'chip-chop'); only the Bedfordshire key describes this, with no numbers for the two types, so one call is drawn. Peak can be at or below 20 kHz in the lower calls and up to the mid 20s in the higher ones. The Bristol page and the Raleigh table agree only loosely on duration (19.6 ms against a 4 to 20 ms range), so duration is the least certain number here. Interval 200 ms is the overlap of the 140 to 230 ms table range and the key's 3 to 6 calls a second; the Bristol mean was much slower (336 ms). Start frequency left out (no second source); the shape's first point (24 kHz) is a drawing choice. Leisler's bat is easily confused with it.

notes: Peak sits in the flat tail. Calls near 52 kHz or higher point to the soprano pipistrelle, and calls near 40 kHz or lower to Nathusius' pipistrelle, so the three overlap at the edges. In open air the call is longer with less sweep and a slower rate; in clutter it is shorter with a faster rate. Left out for lack of a second source: start frequency, and min/max of duration and interval. The shape's first point (55 kHz) comes from one measured value in the Bristol page and is probably lower than the start seen on modern full-spectrum recordings. Duration 6 ms is one measured mean that the second table's 2.5 to 7.5 ms range contains. End 45 kHz rests on the Bristol minimum frequency and on the key's statement that the loudest part is the tail at 43 to 46 kHz.

notes: Long constant-frequency part with a very short rise at the start and a short drop at the end. Only the constant-frequency value is sourced (the key says just above 80 kHz; the Iberian key says 75 to 85 kHz). Duration, interval, start and end are left out: no second numeric source was found, and the first and last shape points are illustrative. Real calls shift a few kHz with Doppler compensation, so the constant part varies between individuals. The lesser horseshoe bat is much higher (about 110 kHz).
